entities.name: Jan Roháč of Dubá
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Roháč of Dubá, a Bohemian Hussite general and nobleman, emerged as one of the most steadfast and uncompromising leaders of the radical Hussite faction, the Taborites, in the final tumultuous phase of the Hussite Wars (1419–1434). His defiance, particularly after the decisive defeat of the Taborite forces at the Battle of Lipany in 1434, solidified his image as a symbol of unyielding resistance against both Catholic imperial power and the moderate Utraquist Hussites. His life and dramatic end represent the last gasp of the radical Hussite dream for a truly reformed Bohemian society, profoundly influencing the memory of the Hussite movement within Czech national consciousness.

Following the catastrophic defeat at Lipany, where the Taborite army was largely annihilated, Jan Roháč refused to accept the Compacts of Basel, the agreement between moderate Hussites and the Catholic Church, which he viewed as a betrayal of Jan Hus's original tenets. He retreated to his fortified stronghold, Sion Castle, near Kutná Hora, gathering remnants of the radical Hussite forces and continuing a guerrilla campaign. This final act of rebellion provoked a major siege in 1437, led by the forces of the newly crowned King Sigismund of Luxembourg. Despite a valiant defense, Sion Castle fell after a prolonged assault, and Roháč was captured.

His capture and subsequent execution by hanging in Prague on September 18, 1437, marked the definitive end of organized radical Hussite military resistance. While the moderate Utraquist wing of Hussitism continued to exist legally for decades, Roháč's demise closed the chapter on the revolutionary, militant phase of the Hussite Wars, allowing for a period of consolidation and political compromise within Bohemia. His legacy, however, transcended his military defeat, transforming him into a martyr and a potent symbol of national self-determination and religious conviction against overwhelming odds.

entities.name: Jan Roháč of Dubá
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Roháč of Dubá (c. 1400 – September 18, 1437) emerged as a defiant and unyielding Bohemian Hussite general, a figure who epitomized the radical Taborite resistance in the aftermath of the Hussite Wars. Descending from the Bohemian gentry, Roháč became a symbol of unwavering commitment to the Hussite cause, even as the movement fractured and its main forces were defeated. His tenacious holdout against the combined might of Imperial and moderate Hussite forces solidified his place as a tragic hero and a final, uncompromised voice of the Hussite revolution, influencing both popular memory and subsequent national narratives in Bohemia.

Following the catastrophic defeat of the radical Hussites at the Battle of Lipany in 1434, which decimated the Taborite field army, Roháč refused to accept the Basel Compacts or the authority of Emperor Sigismund of Luxembourg. He retreated to his fortified stronghold, Sion Castle near Kutná Hora, where he continued to rally remnants of the radical Hussite faithful. From Sion, he led guerrilla raids and maintained a challenging presence against the newly dominant alliance of Catholic and moderate Utraquist forces. His defiance culminated in a four-month siege of Sion Castle in 1437, led by the experienced Oldřich of Rožmberk, which eventually fell due to overwhelming numbers and superior siege technology.

Roháč's capture and subsequent execution by hanging in Prague, ordered by Emperor Sigismund, sent a clear message about the end of organized Hussite military resistance and the reassertion of royal authority in Bohemia. His death effectively closed the chapter on the Hussite Wars' most radical phase, paving the way for a more stable, albeit religiously complex, political landscape under the Utraquist nobility. His martyrdom, however, ensured his enduring legacy as a symbol of national independence and religious conviction, inspiring later generations of Czech patriots.
